ABSTRACT: Herein, we developed the new, powerful, and easy-to-handle chemical reagent, dimethoxyacetaldehyde-N-
triftosylhydrazone (DMHz-Tfs), as a convenient in situ source of dimethoxydiazoethane under mild conditions. We demonstrate
the carbene reactivity of DMHz-Tfs in iron-catalyzed cyclopropanation and Doyle−Kirmse reactions, providing access to diverse
acetal functionalized cyclopropanes and homoallylic- and allenyl-sulfides at gram-scale with high stereoselectivity. DFT calculations
elucidated the involvement of the most stable doublet spin state iron-carbene intermediate over other possible spin states.

diazo compound, in 1894,

applications have expanded rapidly.

modern organic synthesis.
4

diazomethane to increase functionality and selectivity in
chemical reactions have attracted more attention owing to its
rich and tunable reactivity profile and its ability to prepare
diverse functionalized chemical entities.

The history of dimethoxydiazoethane goes back to 1980
when Abdallah and Gre ́e synthesized it from 2,2-dimethox-
yethylamine in three steps and studied its reactivity as 1,3-
dipoles to prepare acetal/formyl cyclopropanes and pyra-

17

synthesis protocol from the same starting materials without
using N
2

18
Nonetheless, the need for multistep
procedures, hazardous reagents, and acidic conditions limited
its broad applicability. Moreover, the carbene reactivity of
dimethoxydiazoethane has yet to be studied. Hence, the design
and development of a new diazo surrogate that is able to
release dimethoxydiazoethane species under mild conditions
could greatly improve the reagent’s synthetic accessibility,
especially for large-scale applications. In pursuit of our
continuous research efforts in the synthesis and applications
of functionalized diazo alkanes derived from easily decom-
posable N-triftosylhydrazones,
19
we here introduce dimethox-
yacetaldehyde-N-triftosylhydrazone (DMHz-Tfs) as the shelf-
stable and safe-to-handle in situ precursor of dimethoxydiazo-
ethane. The carbene reactivity of DMHz-Tfs was demonstrated
through the iron-catalyzed cyclopropanation of alkenes and
Doyle−Kirmse reaction with allyl and propargyl sulfides
(Figure 1C), allowing access to diverse acetal functionalized
cyclopropanes as well as homoallylic and allenyl sulfides in
high yields with broad scope and excellent functional group
compatibility.
Three dimethoxyacetaldehyde-N-sulfonylhydrazones with
different sulfonyl groups could be readily prepared from
commercially available 2,2-dimethoxyacetaldehyde in excellent
yields (Scheme 1). These reagents are bench-stable crystalline
solids that can be stored at ambient conditions for at least 3
weeks without significant degradation.

Following extensive screening of the reaction conditions, it
was observed that the Fe-catalyzed system was effective in the
cyclopropanation of DMHz-Tfs (Supporting Information
Table S1). With the optimized conditions in hand, we next
examined the scope of alkenes for iron-catalyzed cyclo-
propanation with DMHz-Tfs (1, Scheme 2). Various styrenes
bearing electron-donating (e.g., methyl, methoxy, tert-butyl,
benzene, and benzyl ether) and electron-withdrawing (e.g.,
halogens, trifluoromethyl, nitro, cyano, and ester) groups were
well tolerated, delivering the desired trans-cyclopropanes 4−20
in 72−98% yields. Notably, the electronic properties of the aryl
rings had a negligible effect on the reaction efficiency. For
ortho-substituted styrenes, the yield of the fluorine-substituted
substrate was higher than methyl- and benzyl ether-substituted
substrates (20 vs 18 and 19). Similarly, di- and tri-substituted
styrenes as substrates could give the desired acetal cyclo-
propanes 21−23 in good yields. The reaction conditions were
also applicable to fused aryl substrates (e.g., naphthalene and

selectivity. In addition to aryl alkenes, aliphatic alkenes, such as
enol ether and vinylcyclohexane, were amenable, furnishing the
desired products 36 and 37 in 94% and 49% yields,
respectively. The olefin substrate bearing other alkyl
substituents afforded the corresponding cyclopropane products
in very low yields (see Supporting Information). The reaction
also tolerated p-divinylbenzene, which afforded the desired
biscyclopropane 38 by doubling other reagents. Late-stage
modification of complex molecules, such as 7-hydroxycoumar-
in, fenofibrate, and estrone derivatives, could also be achieved
in good yields with excellent stereocontrol (39−41),
demonstrating the potential for the discovery of more
promising drug candidates.
To highlight the potential utility of this protocol, we scaled
up the reaction of DMHz-Tfs and styrene to a 5 mmol scale,
affording the acetal cyclopropane 3 in good yields without
erosion of stereoselectivity. Then mild acid hydrolysis of 3
provided the formyl cyclopropane 42 in 91% yield, which
could transform into structurally diverse cyclopropane scaffolds
(Scheme 3). For example, oxidation of 42 with KHSO
5
led to
the formation of carboxylic acid 43, while it was reduced to
primary alcohol 44 with NaBH
4
. Cyclopropanecarbonitrile 45
was also obtained smoothly by treating 42 with hydroxylamine
hydrochloride. Finally, the nucleophilic addition of ethynyl-
magnesium bromide to formyl cyclopropane 42 gave a
diastereomeric mixture of propargyl alcohols 46 in 86% yield.
Next, we explored the reactivity of DMHz-Tfs in the Doyle−
Kirmse reaction�an interesting [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrange-
ment reaction to construct C−S and C−C bonds.
20
We chose
DMHz-Tfs and allyl phenyl sulfide as model substrates to
optimize the reaction conditions. After a series of exper-
imentations, we were pleased to find that the target product 49
could be isolated in 95% yield when reacting 1 with allyl
phenyl sulfide in the presence of Fe(TPP)Cl catalyst and
Cs
2
CO
3
base in THF at 40 °C for 12 h under nitrogen
atmosphere (see Supporting Information Table S2 for details).
Under the optimized conditions, the generality of the
reaction was then examined (Scheme 4A). A wide range of aryl
allyl sulfides containing either electron-donating or electron-
withdrawing substituents at the para- or meta-positions of the
aromatic ring were compatible, affording corresponding
products 50−57 in 63 to 98% yields. The steric hindrance
on the aromatic ring impacted the product yields, as ortho-
substituted aryl allyl sulfides produced slightly lower yields
(58−60). The reaction was also amenable to disubstituted aryl
allyl sulfides to deliver the desired products in moderate to
good yields (61−63). Allyl sulfides bearing electron-rich
naphthalene and furan rings smoothly participated in the
process, delivering 64 and 65 in 59% and 58% yields,
respectively. Besides aryl allyl sulfides, methyl, benzyl, and
adamantyl allyl sulfides were also suitable for this conversion,
which could react with DMHz-Tfs to obtain corresponding
products 66−68 in moderate to good yields. Similarly, the
reaction using 2-methylallyl, 1-phenylallyl, and 1,1-dimethy-
lallyl aryl sulfides was also attempted, furnishing the desired
products in moderate to good yield (69−71). It is worth
noting that diallyl sulfide can effectively engage in the reaction,
yielding the desired bilateral [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
product 72 (98% yield and d.r. = 1.5:1) by doubling other
reagents.
We then expanded the scope of this reaction to propargyl
sulfides 48 (Scheme 4B), which offered a convenient route to
functionalized allenes.
21
Aryl propargyl sulfides bearing a
methyl or methoxy group at the para-position of the aryl ring
and naphthyl propargyl sulfide could be converted smoothly
into the corresponding allenyl sulfides 73−76 in moderate to
good yields (49−68%). The reaction could proceed effectively
with 1-methyl or 1-trimethylsilyl substituted alkynyl sulfides,
which delivered target products 77 and 78 in 96% and 91%
yield, respectively. Finally, we explored the versatility of the
acetal-substituted homoallyl sulfide product 49. The mild acid
hydrolysis of 49 produced the corresponding aldehyde analog
79 (92% yield), which then was oxidized in the presence of m-
CPBA to give sulfone derivative 80 in 90% yield (Scheme 4C).

In this work, we developed a new chemical reagent, DMHz-
Tfs, which could slowly release dimethoxydiazoethane in situ
under mild conditions. Its carbene reactivity was established in
iron-catalyzed cyclopropanation and Doyle−Kirmse reactions,
enabling access to various acetal functionalized cyclopropanes
and homoallyl- and allenyl-sulfides. The broad applicability of
the developed protocol was highlighted by the late-stage
modification of complex bioactive molecules, gram-scale
synthesis, and structural diversification of acetal functionalized
products. DFT studies disclosed that the doublet spin state of
the iron catalyst enabled the carbene transfer process. Given its
ease of preparation, high stability, and operational safety,
DMHz-Tfs are expected to have a high potential for carbene
transfer reactions.

ABSTRACT: Herein, we developed the new, powerful, and easy-to-handle chemical reagent, dimethoxyacetaldehyde-N-
triftosylhydrazone (DMHz-Tfs), as a convenient in situ source of dimethoxydiazoethane under mild conditions. We demonstrate
the carbene reactivity of DMHz-Tfs in iron-catalyzed cyclopropanation and Doyle−Kirmse reactions, providing access to diverse
acetal functionalized cyclopropanes and homoallylic- and allenyl-sulfides at gram-scale with high stereoselectivity. DFT calculations
elucidated the involvement of the most stable doublet spin state iron-carbene intermediate over other possible spin states.

In this work, we developed a new chemical reagent, DMHz-
Tfs, which could slowly release dimethoxydiazoethane in situ
under mild conditions. Its carbene reactivity was established in
iron-catalyzed cyclopropanation and Doyle−Kirmse reactions,
enabling access to various acetal functionalized cyclopropanes
and homoallyl- and allenyl-sulfides. The broad applicability of
the developed protocol was highlighted by the late-stage
modification of complex bioactive molecules, gram-scale
synthesis, and structural diversification of acetal functionalized
products. DFT studies disclosed that the doublet spin state of
the iron catalyst enabled the carbene transfer process. Given its
ease of preparation, high stability, and operational safety,
DMHz-Tfs are expected to have a high potential for carbene
transfer reactions.
